summary: A survey of which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP, this edition run in February 1983. It continues a series by David Smallberg. Replaced by RFC 845.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on every computer's door to see which would answer. This is one week's tally.

questions: how many hosts supported tcp in 1983
subtitle: A snapshot of TCP adoption across 329 networked computers in February 1983.

tldr.problem: It was unclear which computers on the early Internet actually supported TCP and the associated protocols Telnet, FTP, and SMTP, which were the foundation of network services.
tldr.mechanism: Someone systematically tested each computer on the network to see whether it would accept TCP connections on these three services, recording whether the connection succeeded, was refused, was unreachable, or the host was dead.
tldr.outcome: This survey showed that out of 329 hosts on the network, about 187 accepted Telnet, 174 accepted FTP, and 170 accepted SMTP, proving that TCP-based services were becoming common. Later surveys (RFC 845) superseded this data.

today: RFC 843 was superseded by RFC 845, a later survey. The RFC is now Historic and serves only as a historical record of the early Internet's adoption of TCP services in early 1983.

sections.title: Survey Overview
sections.content:
RFC 843 documents the results of a survey run by David Smallberg on February 8-9, 1983, testing connectivity to computers on the early Internet. The survey used the NIC hostname table from February 3, 1983, and systematically attempted to connect to 329 hosts using TCP, testing three major services: Telnet, FTP (File Transfer Protocol), and SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol).

This was one in a series of surveys, with the goal of tracking which systems in the network community were actually running and supporting these critical protocols.
sections.eli5: A researcher picked 329 computers from a list of networked machines and knocked on their doors to see if they were awake and willing to talk.

sections.title: Testing Method
sections.content:
The survey used the NIC hostname table to identify computers and their claimed capabilities. Each host entry listed what TCP services it claimed to support: T for TCP (generic), t for Telnet, f for FTP, s for SMTP. Tests ran from 10 am to 5:10 pm PST on February 8, and 1 am to 5:15 am PST on February 9, all from ISI-VAXA.ARPA. Hosts that did not respond or refused connections were retried the next day.

For each service, the survey recorded five possible outcomes: the host did not claim to support the service, the host was unreachable, the connection was refused, the host appeared dead, or the connection was accepted.
sections.eli5: For each computer and each service, the tester recorded what happened: did it say yes, no, stay silent, break the connection, or disappear?

sections.title: Results by Service
sections.content:
Out of 329 hosts tested, the summary tables show adoption across three services. For Telnet: 165 hosts accepted connections, 10 were unreachable, 3 refused, 16 were dead, and 72 did not claim to support it. For FTP: 150 accepted (with 24 allowing anonymous access), 10 unreachable, 2 refused, 15 dead, 80 did not claim support. For SMTP: 134 accepted, 10 unreachable, 2 refused, 14 dead, and 82 did not claim support.

The results reveal that while many hosts claimed support for these services, not all of them worked reliably. Some were offline, some refused connections unexpectedly, and others proved unreachable due to network issues.
sections.eli5: About half the computers worked for Telnet and FTP when tested, but a quarter were either broken, not listening, or unplugged. A few let strangers log in and copy files without passwords.

sections.title: Data Presentation
sections.content:
The RFC presents the detailed results in two orders. The first listing is alphabetical by hostname, showing for each machine its IP address, its claimed TCP services, and the test result for each of the three services (accepted, refused, unreachable, or dead). The second listing is in the order of the NIC host table, providing the same information in a different sequence for cross-reference.

This dual presentation allowed readers to quickly look up individual machines either by name or by their table position, making it easier to find and interpret results.
sections.eli5: The data is listed twice: once in ABC order so you can search by name, and once in the original computer list order for reference.

sections.title: Network State
sections.content:
The survey provides a valuable snapshot of Internet readiness in early 1983. Major research institutions and defense contractors are well represented, with sites like CMU, Xerox, BBN, and various defense research facilities showing strong support for TCP services. The presence of 150+ hosts accepting FTP and 165+ accepting Telnet demonstrates that these protocols were becoming the de facto standard for remote access and file transfer, even at this early stage.

The survey also reveals systemic issues: approximately 51 hosts appear completely dead, 15 are unreachable (possibly behind poor network links), and a non-trivial number claim support for a service but refuse connections. This variability underscores the immature state of the deployed infrastructure in 1983.
sections.eli5: The Internet in 1983 had hundreds of computers working, but about a fifth were broken, gone offline, or just not listening. A few big research places had all their machines working well.

references.text: Smallberg, D., "Who Talks TCP? Survey of 8 February 1983", RFC 843, February 1983.
